item.title: Limtiaco, Moylan outline differing approaches in congressional debate

item.content:encoded:
Alicia Limtiaco and Del. James Moylan outlined their priorities for Guam during a Guam Chamber of Commerce congressional debate ahead of the Nov. 3 general election.

Both candidates said Guam needs relief from high living costs, better access to federal funding and benefits, stronger infrastructure, and more economic opportunities. Both candidates also supported addressing the Jones Act’s impact on Guam’s shipping costs, expanding air service and competition, improving access to federal benefits, and returning unused federal land for local use. However, they offered different approaches to addressing those concerns.

Limtiaco, a former Guam attorney general and U.S. attorney, said her campaign would focus on fairness for Guam in federal programs, accountability for government spending, and creating more opportunities for local businesses and workers.

Limtiaco said she would push for more affordable housing by helping restore vacant or deteriorating homes through existing federal housing programs. To improve accountability, Limtiaco proposed tracking federal funding and project progress through public updates, as well as using congressional hearings and oversight to address delays or misuse of funds.

“I will establish a Guam Business and Economic Advisory Council to bring your experience into our congressional office, and I will report back on what has moved, what funding has been approved, and where work remains,” Limtiaco said.

Moylan emphasized his record in Congress and the federal funding and legislation he said he has helped secure for Guam. He said he would continue working to reduce barriers for local businesses, expand workforce opportunities, and pursue changes to shipping and air travel policies.

“These are real investments in the safety and well-being of our people, and I welcome the scrutiny,” Moylan said. “My commitment to serving you began long before this election. I served through the pandemic, through the devastation of Typhoon Mawar, and challenges that followed. Public service is a responsibility.”

On shipping, Moylan said he has introduced measures seeking exemptions from the Jones Act for Guam, including for fuel and emergencies. He said he would continue pushing a permanent exemption, while Limtiaco called for a broader review of how the law affects Guam and what changes would best address the island’s needs.

“I have already introduced with Congressman Ed Case from Hawaii over 11 measures that address the Jones Act exception specifically for Guam regarding fuel, regarding emergency situations,” Moylan said. “President Trump has extended the temporary Jones Act exception going on the seventh time. This is the opportunity where we can come together, people of quant, to present our argument even greater before Congress, before Senate, and get that permanent exception we need.”

Both candidates also support improving air connections to Guam and expanding tourism. Moylan highlighted his proposed Pacific Island Flight Alternatives Act, which he said would allow airlines from countries such as Japan, South Korea, and the Philippines to bring visitors to the Marianas and connect them to the U.S. mainland. He also supports a visa-waiver program for visitors from the Philippines.

Limtiaco said she would work with federal agencies, airlines, and industry representatives to find ways to improve air services and address policies that limit competition. She also identified the Philippines as a priority market for a visa-waiver program, citing potential benefits for tourism and the workforce.

The candidates agreed that Guam should receive better access to federal benefits, including Supplemental Security Income and improved Medicaid funding.

Moylan said he would continue pushing legislation to extend SSI to Guam and address limits on federal Medicaid funding. Limtiaco also supports SSI eligibility for Guam residents and removing Guam’s Medicaid funding cap. She said that, if the cap cannot be removed, she would seek adjustments that better reflect the cost of medical care and the number of people needing services.

On the military buildup, Limtiaco said Guam’s civilian community should benefit from federal investments and have a clearer picture of how funding is being spent and when projects will be completed. She identified the power grid, water system, roads, housing, education, and public services as areas needing attention.

Moylan pointed to federal military construction funding and community projects he said he has helped secure, including funding for roads, emergency facilities, and public safety vehicles. He argued that investments supporting infrastructure and pubic services outside military installations also benefit Guam residents.

In their discussion on jobs and workforce needs, Limtiaco identified ship repair as an area that could help diversify Guam’s economy, create jobs, and provide opportunities beyond the military buildup.

Moylan highlighted efforts to extend the H-2B temporary worker program through 2035 and support workforce training. He also pointed to legislation intended to reduce college tuition costs for students in U.S. territories, which he said had passed the House and was awaiting Senate action.

Both candidates said unused federal land should be returned for local use.

In her closing statement, Limtiaco said she would focus on fair treatment in federal programs, stronger infrastructure, and creating more opportunities for Guam’s residents and businesses.

Moylan closed by emphasizing experience, reliability, and following through on commitments. He said he has secured federal investments for Guam but acknowledged that more work remains.

The general election is scheduled for Tuesday.

item.title: CNMI voters head to polls early; runoff plans already underway
item.description: A steady stream of voters lined up Tuesday at the Multi-Purpose Center on Saipan as early voting for the 2026 CNMI general election got underway across the Commonwealth, kicking off a seven-day advance voting period ahead of the Nov. 3 election. item.content:encoded:
A steady stream of voters lined up Tuesday at the Multi-Purpose Center on Saipan as early voting for the 2026 CNMI general election got underway across the Commonwealth, kicking off a seven-day advance voting period ahead of the Nov. 3 election.

Early voting is being conducted on Saipan, Tinian and Rota, giving voters an opportunity to cast ballots before Election Day. On Saipan, voting is taking place at the Multi-Purpose Center, while Tinian voters may vote at the Tinian Youth Center and Rota voters at Northern Marianas College Room B-2.

Commonwealth Election Commission Executive Director Kayla Igitol Magofna said election officials are prepared for what is expected to be a busy election season and are also developing contingency plans should any race require a runoff election.

"Yes, still we're doing that," Magofna said when asked whether the commission is preparing for a possible runoff.

Under Commonwealth law, a runoff election may be required if no candidate secures the vote threshold necessary for an outright victory. Election officials say the possibility remains particularly significant in the gubernatorial and attorney general races.

The gubernatorial contest featured former Gov. Ralph Torres and running mate Benjamin Jones Jr. against independent tickets headed by Rep. Jonathan "BJ" Attao and House Speaker Edmund Villagomez, as well as former Education Commissioner Lawrence Camacho and former Senate President Edith Deleon Guerrero.

Meanwhile, attorneys Joaquin "Jack" Torres, Jonathan "Robbie" Glass and Michael Evangelista are competing in the attorney general race, which will determine only the second elected attorney general in CNMI history.

Magofna said ballots cast during the general election will be tabulated using voting machines. If a runoff becomes necessary, however, election officials may hand-count ballots because runoff ballots likely would be printed locally.

"The hand counting, we probably will do that during the runoff because we're probably going to print runoff ballots on the island," she said.

Election officials are also reminding voters to bring valid identification, complete the required early-voting application and carefully review both sides of their ballots before casting them.

As of Sept. 19, the Commonwealth had 18,521 registered voters eligible to participate in the election.

Key election dates include the early voting period from Oct. 27 through Nov. 2 and General Election Day on Nov. 3. A runoff election will be scheduled following certification of results if required under Commonwealth election law.

item.title: CPUC to decide Thursday on Eastern Power solar project
item.description: The Commonwealth Public Utilities Commission is expected to decide Thursday whether to approve Eastern Power Solutions' proposed multimillion-dollar solar and battery storage project after completing a final review of the agreement and public feedback. item.content:encoded:
The Commonwealth Public Utilities Commission is expected to decide Thursday whether to approve Eastern Power Solutions' proposed multimillion-dollar solar and battery storage project after completing a final review of the agreement and public feedback.

Acting Chairman Bruce Camacho said commissioners are conducting one last review of the power purchase agreement and have been evaluating roughly 50 written comments submitted by members of the public.

"The Commission is conducting one final review of the contract and power purchase agreement," Camacho said. "Commissioners have also been sharing the written public comments received individually, and we are carefully reviewing approximately 50 submissions received thus far."

The anticipated decision comes as Eastern Power Solutions has warned that it could withdraw its proposal if regulators fail to act before Oct. 31, citing time-sensitive federal financing incentives tied to the project.

Camacho said the commission has also received a letter from Gov. David Apatang urging regulators to expedite their review. He said the governor reiterated his support for the project during a recent conversation.

"We acknowledge receipt of Gov. Apatang's letter urging the Commission to expedite its review," Camacho said. "I informed him that the Commission intends to convene at the earliest opportunity, Thursday, Oct. 29, to render a decision."

The governor and project supporters have argued that delays could jeopardize financing opportunities and federal tax credits viewed as critical to the project's success.

Among the public comments reviewed by commissioners were concerns about environmental and historic preservation issues. One commenter referenced controversy surrounding Guam's Mangilao solar farm and impacts on Marbo Cave.

Camacho said those concerns are being taken seriously but expressed confidence in the environmental review process.

"These concerns deserve serious consideration, particularly given the scale and long-term nature of the proposed project," he said.

Camacho added that revisions addressing liability and litigation concerns have clarified legal responsibilities between the parties involved. He also noted that any required environmental reviews, consultations and permits must be completed before project activities proceed.

While emphasizing that protecting ratepayers remains the commission's primary responsibility, Camacho said regulators recognize the potential benefits of renewable energy.

"I want to emphasize that the Commission is not attempting to delay this project unnecessarily," he said. "We recognize the potential benefits of renewable energy, including reducing our dependence on imported fossil fuels and providing greater long-term energy price stability for the people of Saipan, Tinian and Rota."

At the same time, Camacho said the proposed agreement represents a significant long-term commitment.

"However, this is a 25-year contractual commitment, and the Commission has a statutory responsibility to ensure that its decision is informed, legally sound and in the best interests of the Commonwealth," he said.

The commission is expected to announce its decision this Thursday.

item.content:encoded:
As prices have ticked up in recent years, the cost to caregivers has skyrocketed. A study, released Wednesday by AARP , finds that family caregivers — people helping out disabled, chronically ill or elderly adults — now spend an average $11,508 out of pocket each year. That's roughly 60% more than just five years ago, and adds up to 31% of a caregiver's income, on average.

The increase during those years is more than twice the overall rate of inflation of 24%, as measured by the federal Bureau of Labor Statistics' Consumer Price Index.

What's driving the ramp-up? Food, housing and medical expenses are the biggest chunk, finds the study, which queried 2,538 family caregivers.

The bump in costs comes as family caregivers take on more care and more complicated medical responsibilities at home, says Megan O'Reilly, vice president of governmental affairs at AARP. "The more care that's needed, the more it costs."

And increased spending is only part of the story. The demands of caregiving often require people to reduce their working hours or quit work entirely, the survey finds. It's a double whammy: increased costs on top of lost income.

Meghan Maher has seen that first-hand. Just seven weeks after the birth of her first baby, her mother was diagnosed with advanced cancer. Suddenly, Maher was a "sandwich" caregiver — parent and child needing her at the same time.

At first, she tried to manage it all. She returned to her career in cancer research after maternity leave, but keeping up with the demands of work, her mom and her newborn son was too much.

She shrank her hours to part time. But even that wasn't manageable. There was no way to attend all her mother's appointments, coordinate her care, and also be available for big deadlines on the job.

She quit, and the family's income fell by half. Because her husband had a good job, they weren't struggling, but "it was definitely scary," she says now. As her mom got sicker her parents moved in, increasing the household expenses.

Soon after her mother's death in 2017, her father had a series of major complications from abdominal surgery and was critically ill for months. Maher needed to be by his side during hospital stays, advocating for him on a moment's notice, so now the family also needed to pay for child care. She estimates the cost at about $10,000 a year.

Her father eventually recovered, and the family was able to manage despite the difficulties. Many aren't so lucky.

About half of all family caregivers say they've made major financial sacrifices, according to the AARP report: Working more hours, cutting savings, or even drawing down on money put away for retirement.

Many Americans deal with the cost of care, and more will in the future. About 63 million people now provide ongoing help for a family member or friend — roughly 1 in 4 adults. The need will likely grow: An estimated 70 percent of the people turning 65 today will need some form of help as they age.

Medicare does not pay for routine help either at home or in a facility, and that care is expensive. In 2025, 40 hours of in-home caregiving help a week ran about $72,792 a year, according to the insurance company Genworth, which conducts annual surveys of the cost of care. Skilled nursing costs an average of $115,000 per year for a shared room.

When Maher returned to work, she became a professional death doula. That means she helps clients with the emotional and practical challenges at the end of life. She's self-employed, so she can control her own schedule and limit the number of clients she serves. It allows her the flexibility to help her father as he ages. But her income is half what it would have been in her old career.

With the clients she helps, she sees other ways that care costs pile up. In Florida where she lives, it's routine for chronically ill people to hire an attorney in order to qualify for Medicaid, which unlike Medicare does foot the bill for long-term care. Even though they are eligible for the benefits, the paperwork is so complex that they wind up paying for legal help to navigate it. In Florida, she says, that runs about $6,000.

What she has seen and experienced motivates her to call attention to the caregiving crunch. In April, Maher testified before Congress at a special Senate committee on aging. "Caregiving has also reshaped my professional life," she said on the Senate floor. "The flexibility of self-employment comes with real financial and professional tradeoffs." She was invited by Daughterhood , an organization that offers support and resources for caregivers.

Family caregivers can access some public money, depending on where they live. All states pay some types of family caregivers through Medicaid. In California, for instance, more than 800,000 caregivers earn between $16.90 and $25 an hour for in-home work. Funds for these programs are likely to dwindle due to President Trump's big budget bill that cut nearly $1 trillion out of Medicaid funding over the next decade.

If the person who needs care is eligible for Veterans Administration benefits, they may also be entitled to financial help to cover the cost of caregiving. Like Medicaid, the rules are complex, and many family caregivers hire advocates to advise on eligibility and the application procedure.

The cost of care hasn't been as visible as the cost of gasoline, food and healthcare, says AARP executive vice president Nancy LeaMond. She believes that will change. "When you see the number of people paying this kind of money, I think that'll be an impetus for action in the legislative arena."

In the last few years, Congress has introduced various proposals that could put some money back into the pockets of caregivers, such as allowing caregivers to spend money from their tax-sheltered health savings accounts on their parents' medical expenses. In some states, new rules are already a reality.

Six states now offer tax credits to family caregivers for expenses like retrofitting a home with grab bars or railings, usually between $1,000 and $5,000 a year. Two other states have more limited programs. Last year, two U.S. Senators introduced a bipartisan bill that would establish a similar $5,000 tax credit nationwide.

In 14 states and the District of Columbia, most employers are required to offer paid family and medical leave. Those policies include time off for caregiving for a family member. Another bill introduced into Congress would convert that into a national policy that would require up to 12 weeks of partly paid leave for some workers.

A third proposed federal law would protect the Social Security benefits of caregivers. Under current rules, a person who stops working in order to care full-time for family sees their future Social Security check shrink, because they are no longer earning credits toward retirement. This bill would change the law to continue awarding points to full-time caregivers.

"We spend a lot of time talking to members of Congress, and you can't raise this issue in a meeting without being interrupted by someone telling their own story," says LeaMond. "In time, I believe that will coalesce to support family caregiving."

Kat McGowan is an independent journalist covering adult caregiving who reports the series " What It Takes " for NPR.

item.title: Dozens are dead in a high-speed train crash in Spain
item.description: Updated October 28, 2026 at 11:53 PM ChST URDA, Spain — A high-speed train slammed into the rear of another train that had stopped, derailing two cars and killing at least 64 people on Wednesday in central Spain, authorities said.
item.content:encoded:
Updated October 28, 2026 at 11:53 PM ChST

URDA, Spain — A high-speed train slammed into the rear of another train that had stopped, derailing two cars and killing at least 64 people on Wednesday in central Spain, authorities said.

The central government's office for Castilla La Mancha confirmed the death toll had risen.

The regional president of Castilla La Mancha, Emiliano García-Page, had said at least 80 people were injured as rescue workers continue to search in the wreckage for survivors and bodies.

It was the second major train accident in Spain this year.

Spain's rail system operator ADIF said the crash occurred Wednesday morning in the province of Toledo. The accident was between two high-speed trains carrying hundreds of passengers and heading in the same direction from the capital Madrid to Seville in southwestern Spain, according to Esther Padilla, spokesperson for the Castilla La Mancha region.

One ran into the tail of the other that had stopped, knocking two of its cars off the track.

Padilla said that the cause of the crash was not known. Rail service was suspended between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia.

The crash, which occurred in a flat stretch surrounded by olive fields in between the towns of Urda and Los Yébenes, left one car shredded into bits of metal and other material, scattering debris down a gravel slope.

Spanish Health Minister Mónica García said that emergency workers were focusing on rescuing survivors and bodies from the two most damaged train cars. She said that the injured are being sent to different hospitals in the area.

"It was a high-speed impact, so we are expecting this to be a tragedy," García said.

The accident involved a train from Spain's state-owned RENFE company and the private rail company IRYO. It appeared the RENFE train rammed the IRYO train, Spanish media reported. García-Page said 24 died in the RENFE train, and six in the IRYO one.

Passenger Ignacio Relaño was traveling on the RENFE train. He told state broadcaster TVE that the train had stopped momentarily on the line before it started again and then crashed into the IRYO.

"We all felt the train abruptly slowing down and then the impact," he said. "The car leaned to one side like it was about to tip over. I hit my nose, everything went flying, luggage, cell phones. Everything shook."

Padilla said that 397 passengers were in the RENFE train and 147 passengers in the IRYO train.

Trains from those two companies were also involved in a deadly crash in January.

IRYO, an Italian-owned company, said in a statement that it has "activated its security protocols and is closely working with authorities."

The mayor of the nearby town of Urda, Manuel Galán, said that that civil protection authorities had asked his town hall to prepare a sports pavilion to attend to injured passengers.

A military emergency brigade was deployed to help emergency services, firefighters and police. Ambulances and medical helicopters made trips to and from the site, while unscathed survivors were put on buses.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez canceled his agenda to focus on the crash. He wrote on X that he was "dismayed by the serious train accident in Toledo."

"Emergency services are working on site to attend to the affected passengers," wrote Sánchez, who faces a national election next month. "All my thoughts are with the victims and their families."

Spain's King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia said in a short statement on X that they were following news of the accident.

"We are deeply saddened and concerned by the train accident in Urda (Toledo)," the royal couple said. "We share in the grief of the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives, and we send our heartfelt support to the injured and all those affected."

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said "My heart goes out to the victims' families and loved ones. Today, Europe mourns with you."

Spain's soccer federation postponed all 24 Copa del Rey games scheduled on Wednesday.

The wreckage of Wednesday's crash reminded many of the aftermath of another train collision in January, when 46 people died in southern Spain when a IRYO train jumped the track and hit an oncoming RENFE train. That sent the first two cars of the impacted train plummeting down a four-meter (13-foot) slope.

That crash was the deadliest in Spain since a 2013 crash that killed 80 people.

The January incident shook confidence in the European country's extensive high-speed rail service.

Over recent decades, Spain has invested heavily in high-speed rail — which the country's railway union defines as rails for trains going 250 kph (155 mph) and over — turning it into a world leader.

Spain has laid some 3,900 kilometers (2,400 miles) of such tracks over more than three decades for its 49 million residents. Only China, with 45,000 kilometers (28,000 miles) for its 1.4 billion people, has more high-speed track, according to the International Union of Railways.

item.title: How a lifelong Republican came to lead the data center battle in Ohio
item.description: Updated October 28, 2026 at 11:21 PM ChST Stay up to date with our Politics newsletter, sent weekly .
item.content:encoded:
Updated October 28, 2026 at 11:21 PM ChST

Stay up to date with our Politics newsletter, sent weekly .

MT. ORAB, Ohio — The data center mystery in this rural exurb of Cincinnati has consumed Nick Owens.

The lifelong Republican and self-described small-town attorney has spent countless hours trying to figure out what's going on with 1,000 acres of farmland and trees that property records show were sold to a data center developer in 2024 and 2025.

In a few spots, the data center property runs right up against beautiful two-story homes.

"This is the Ohio that people brag about. This is the Ohio people love. This is the small town charm," he says. "Living in the rural area, but getting the benefits of a nice, lovely neighborhood."

Some of the most coordinated opposition to data centers anywhere in the country grew out of what happened in secrecy in this village of 4,300 people, a short drive up a country road from Owens' home.

Nondisclosure agreements have stymied Owens' efforts to learn more. But along his quest, he crossed paths with another local attorney and a real estate agent who were equally alarmed. Together, they mobilized a network of volunteers in nearly all 88 counties in the state. They are Democrats, Republicans and Independents. They called themselves Conserve Ohio.

"We all share the same ethos and the same passion for preserving our way of life, preserving the future of Ohio, frankly, from the hyperscale data center invasion," says Owens. "It's really beautiful."

This fall, the group is behind ballot initiatives in 10 communities that would amend local charters to prohibit the construction of large-scale data centers — the kind used to power artificial intelligence. It's an effort that goes beyond the temporary pauses that hundreds of municipal and county governments have embraced.

"All too often you hear from the politicians, 'Well, the community should have a say,'" says Owens. "We're going to find out in ten communities whether or not the communities want them."

Meanwhile, the grassroots group is working on a more ambitious undertaking: a petition for an amendment to the state constitution that would ban large-scale data centers statewide. Their goal is to put that to Ohio's voters in 2027.

It's been more than a decade since tech companies first came to Ohio, drawn by the state's inexpensive and abundant land, its energy infrastructure and its generous tax breaks. That combination paved the way for some of the fastest data center growth in the country.

Now, despite the economic benefits — considerable tax revenue, money for schools, numerous construction jobs and a smaller number of permanent jobs — no one seems to want a computing campus in their backyard, especially one shrouded in secrecy.

"Should the school have extra money or the local government have extra money so we have a constant hum and ridiculous amounts of emissions and pollution?" Owens says, pointing out that hyperscale data centers will require new power plants. "Our community is not for sale."

Pressed to consider whether the state should forgo all opportunities, Owens says he'd entertain the idea of putting data centers on old industrial sites, where they'd be buffered from people.

"If we're going to have data centers, those are the prime places," he says, while acknowledging that it'd be cheaper and easier for a developer to build on pristine farmland than on an old coal site. "I don't know if there are enough brownfield sites, but shouldn't we start with those first?"

In recent months, candidates running for statewide office in Ohio have been trying to convince voters that they hear their concerns — even as they stop short of backing the kind of sweeping moratorium data center opponents are seeking.

Conserve Ohio has not endorsed any of them.

Until recently, data center projects weren't all that controversial, in part because they were smaller and weren't being built for AI.

But as the issue has gained traction, it's become a hot topic in the midterms, including in the tight race to fill a U.S. Senate seat. Former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown has cast his opponent, the incumbent Republican Senator Jon Husted, as "the face of data centers." Brown has been reminding voters that as lieutenant governor, Husted welcomed tech companies to Ohio and championed their data center investments.

Meanwhile, Husted has accused Brown of hypocrisy, pointing to Brown's past support for data centers.

Husted has also introduced his own solution, pushing a bill in Congress aimed at getting data centers to pay for power grid upgrades and other costs associated with their massive energy use. Senate Democrats have blocked the bill, calling it toothless, prompting Husted to accuse the Democrats of not caring or helping.

These political gestures have not persuaded Linda Moodie, an independent who's been volunteering with Conserve Ohio. She doesn't trust that any of the candidates running for statewide office "will do the right thing" if elected, which is to give the people a say in the data center buildout.

"It's really something that I think a lot of us didn't see coming, and all of a sudden there's just an influx of them," she says.

While Moodie wonders if all the talk on the campaign trail is simply to get votes, she says she will cast her ballot for Brown, who she thinks has been talking about data centers the longest.

And meanwhile, between now and election day, she's seizing every opportunity to collect signatures to get the statewide ban on the ballot next year.

On a recent evening, she set up a booth at the "Halloween on the Green" celebration in the Cincinnati suburb of Fairfield. She handed out candy to kids and clipboards with the petition to parents. Both were enthusiastically received.

"The closer it hits to home, the more people that are going to want to do something," says Moodie.

Two years ago, Owens served as a Trump delegate at the Republican National Convention. He won't say how he's voting this fall, but he says no doubt the data center issue, along with $6 diesel, have dampened Republican enthusiasm.

item.title: Senate candidates built up massive campaign war chests with out-of-state donations
item.description: 📲 Get the latest on the midterms & more in the NPR App In key U.S. Senate races this year, candidates are soliciting donations from outside of their home states, and their out-of-state messaging is different from what they're running locally.
item.content:encoded:
📲 Get the latest on the midterms & more in the NPR App

In key U.S. Senate races this year, candidates are soliciting donations from outside of their home states, and their out-of-state messaging is different from what they're running locally.

An NPR analysis of Google Ads for four major Senate races — Iowa, Georgia, Ohio and Texas — found that the Democratic and Republican candidates spent more than $15 million on advertising related to fundraising in the 2025-26 election cycle. About three quarters of that went to ads that ran nationally.

Often, these ads focus on national talking points — such as attacking or defending President Trump, or turning the Senate blue or red — rather than local issues. For candidates like Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff and Iowa Democratic nominee Josh Turek, more than 80% of their itemized individual contributions have come from out of state.

The funneling of funds has affected at least four of the competitive Senate races, where a majority of the money is coming from outside the state. ActBlue and WinRed, two major grassroots fundraising platforms, are a major catalyst for out-of-state fundraising.

Because this technology is inexpensive to run, it incentivizes candidates to rely on digital ads, according to Zachary Albert, a professor of politics at Brandeis University.

"ActBlue and WinRed really reduced the transaction costs for contributing," Albert said. "Even if you're only yielding like a $5 or $10 contribution from someone like the costs of soliciting that are so much lower than they used to be, that it makes it worthwhile."

With both parties — and each candidate — now having fundraising platforms, political hopefuls increasingly need to stand out from the crowd and are often shifting their messaging to a broader audience, which can result in using polarizing messaging to solicit funds.

For in-state and out-of-state ads, candidates tend to have two different sets of talking points, according to Wesleyan Media Project's Michael Franz.

"In a general election campaign for a [local] TV ad, a candidate will never say, 'I'm the Democrat,' because they want to appeal to moderates and swing voters and they want voters across the aisle," Franz said. "But with a digital ad that's airing outside of your state, the party label becomes more important."

This is reflected in many digital ads. Former Ohio Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown — who is seeking to regain a place in the Senate — calls to turn his state blue while Georgia Republican Rep. Mike Collins asks people to help turn his state's Senate seat red. Republicans currently control the Senate but there are a number of toss-up races giving Democrats a path to taking back the chamber.

Iowa Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson touts her America First credentials in ads for her Senate race, saying she's "America First," while Ossoff in Georgia attacks Trump directly.

According to Michael Heseltine, a researcher at Oxford University who studies how members of congress use social media to communicate , says while there is a large amount of locally-focused messaging, candidates are increasingly spending more time and energy on national talking points.

"[If] we continue on that trend, you'll probably find more and more members who have neglected their constituencies or at least not presented themselves as representatives of their constituencies," he said.

In a statement to NPR, the Ossoff campaign denied targeting audiences by location, and says the campaign "is powered by small-dollar donors because the Senator refuses donations from corporate PACs and federal lobbyists."

The other campaigns declined to comment or did not respond to interview requests.

Daniel Hopkins, a political science professor at the University of Pennsylvania, believes we're in a new era of campaigning, where candidates now have two major stakeholders to appeal to: a voter base which is local, and a donor base which is often larger and nationwide.

"When Jon Ossoff is trying to compete for votes, he's competing against Georgia Republicans," Hopkins said. "But when Jon Ossoff is trying to compete for dollars, he's competing for attention and for donations, ultimately with other prominent Democratic candidates."

The amount of out-of-state funds for congressional campaigns has been rising each election cycle, according to OpenSecrets .

In order to get these funds, candidates are urged to promote the party platform. Hopkins attributes this to two causes; the party platforms becoming more homogenous and changes in campaign finance laws.

"It used to be that the pathway to success was to rise up through your local party, building the support of local elites in your community," he said.

"The path to political success increasingly goes through a set of, 'ATM districts' around the country that are known to give a lot of money either to Democrats or the Republicans," Hopkins explained.

In states that are dominated by one party, donors might elect to send their funds to a more competitive state to help influence elections, according to Sarah Bryner, a director who studies campaign finance at Public Agenda, a research organization focused on democracy.

"People from California really don't feel like they have much to do because their state's going to go blue regardless," she said. "So they support candidates in states like Georgia or Texas."

While both parties now benefit from out-of-state funds, Democrats tended to rely on them, due to weaker local funding systems in competitive states like Ohio and Michigan. As a result, Democrats built a system for grassroots donations — ActBlue which launched in 2004 — nearly 15 years before Republicans, who launched WinRed in 2019.

While some of the Democratic advantage in out-of-state fundraising can be attributed to Republican incumbents' connections to local funding, part of it can be attributed to the Democratic Party's diverse base of voters.

"You're having to bring together that diverse coalition, not necessarily around some unified ideological agenda, but based on a kind of discrete policy [that] claims to represent particular groups," said Brandeis University's Zachary Albert.

Meanwhile, Republicans were initially slow to realize the potential for small dollar fundraising until Trump.

"The Republicans realized, especially during Trump, that they do have a national audience of small donors ready to activate behind their preferred candidates for their preferred agenda," Public Agenda's Sarah Bryner said.

While some states are trying to limit outside funds, like Hawaii implementing a cap on out-of-state donations starting in 2027 , it's difficult to regulate at a national level, according to University of Massachusetts political science professor Raymond La Raja.
